sections.title: The World of Homer's Odyssey
sections.description:
Homer’s epic poem Odyssey is a foundational text of Western culture and tradition. It is at least 2,800 years old (and in some form probably much older), yet it continues to resonate with us in the 21st century. While interest in the Odyssey has been fairly constant for centuries, it has recently surged on the strength of new translations into English, especially by our very own Professor Emily Wilson, and the current blockbuster film adaptation by Chris Nolan. The public conversation and debate have brought people back to the original tale of adventure, as vibrant and fresh today as when it was first sung so long ago. The Odyssey offers us a window on the values and imaginations of ancient Greeks, so there is plenty of historical interest, but the way the epic is received, translated, and re-presented also reflects how each generation grapples with the same timeless themes. And, just as it was originally intended, the Odyssey should be experienced for pleasure.
In this course we will read Emily Wilson’s translation of the Odyssey in its entirety, while simultaneously learning about the historical and cultural context of its composition. Alongside Wilson’s verse translation we will examine samples of other translations, both verse and prose. We will lean heavily on archaeology to illuminate the real world in which Homer lived, and to sort fact from fiction regarding the Trojan War, the heroic Bronze Age warriors, and the events of Odysseus’ journey home to Ithaca. We will read and view modern and contemporary works adapting or inspired by the Odyssey. The primary aim of the course is to delve into the universal humanity of the story, both within the context of 500 years of Greek history, and the way that it continues to inspire generations of writers, artists, filmmakers, and just regular adults and children. The course content will be augmented by visits to the Penn Museum to examine the material culture of the Greek Bronze and Iron Ages.
